references.text: Jesus says that whoever finds their life will lose it, and whoever loses their life for his sake will find it – the same paradoxical principle of losing and finding life.
Parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus says that whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for his sake will find it.
Parallel passage in Mark where Jesus speaks about how whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for the sake of Jesus and the gospel will save it.
Jesus repeats the same principle in another context in Luke: Whoever seeks to save their life will lose it, and whoever loses it will save it.

Jesus says that whoever loves their life will lose it, and whoever hates their life in this world will keep it for eternal life – the same fundamental principle expressed with slightly different words.
Paul expresses a similar principle: For him, to live is Christ and to die is gain – giving up one's own life for the sake of Christ is actually winning.
Jesus encourages the church in Smyrna to be faithful until death, and he will give them the crown of life – losing one's life for the sake of Christ leads to eternal life.
They overcame the accuser by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, and they did not love their lives even unto death – they were willing to lose their lives and thus won victory.
The preceding verse in the same context where Jesus calls the disciples to deny themselves, take up their cross daily, and follow him – this is the prerequisite for the paradox expressed in verse 24.
